findings.finding: Insights: f(n)=min LCM of three distinct positive integers summing to n. For huge M=3^{2025!}, f(M+c)≈ smallest power‑of‑3 LCM ≥M that can achieve sum M+c using three distinct powers of 3. g(c)=⌊2025!·f(M+c)/M⌋/2025! gives the nearest multiple of 1/2025! ≤f(M+c)/M. Compute g for given c, sum, reduce to p/q, then (p+q) mod 99991. Watch: c may not be representable as sum of two smaller powers of 3, forcing larger LCM (next power of 3). Ensure distinctness and minimal LCM.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n ⇒ minimal L (largest divisor) satisfies n=L+a+b, a,b|L, a≠b. Write a=L/p, b=L/q (p≠q≥2). Then n=L(1+1/p+1/q) ⇒ L=n·pq/(pq+p+q). For given n, choose distinct p,q giving largest 1/p+1/q (smallest p,q) such that denominator D=(pq)/gcd(pq,pq+p+q) divides n. Since n=M+c, M=3^K, K even, M≡1 (mod d) if 3∤d else M≡0. Thus condition: if 3∤D then c≡−1 (mod D); if 3|D then c≡0 (mod D). For each c (0, 4M, 1848374, 10162574, 265710644, 44636594) compute smallest (p,q) meeting condition → ratio r=L/n= pq/(pq+p+q). Then g(c)=⌊2025!·r⌋/2025!. Sum T=∑⌊2025!·r⌋, result =T/2025!. Reduce p/q, output (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure D’s 3‑factor handling, c=4M gives c≡4 (mod D) (since M≡1), and verify p,q distinct. Use small p,q (2,3),(2,5),(2,7),(3,5)… until condition satisfied. Compute with Python for exact T.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N. Minimal ratio LCM/N is 6/11 (when N≡0 mod 11 via (2d,3d,6d)), next 4/7 (when N≡0 mod 7 via (2d,4d,8d)). For N not ≡0 mod 7, ratio >4/7.  

M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡1 (mod 7,11).  

Compute N_i=M+c_i:  
c=0 → N≡1 (mod 7,11) ⇒ ratio >4/7 → floor(2025!*ratio)=⌊2025!*0.6…⌋=⌊0.6·2025!⌋.  
c=4M → N=5M ⇒ N≡5 (mod 7,11) → same ratio >4/7.  
c=1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594 are tiny ⇒ N≡1+ c (mod 7,11). Each ≠0 mod 7,11 → same floor.  

Thus all six g(c)=⌊k·2025!⌋/2025! with same integer k=⌊0.6·2025!⌋. Sum =6·⌊0.6·2025!⌋/2025!. Reduce: numerator=6·⌊0.6·2025!⌋, denominator=2025!. Compute p+q mod 99991. (Key pitfall: ignore tiny ε; only c=4M changes N/M factor.)

Insights: f(n)=min L with three distinct divisors a,b,L, a+b+L=n ⇒ a,b|L. Minimal L uses L’s two largest proper divisors: L/p, L/q (p<q smallest prime factors). Then n=L+L/p+L/q ⇒ L=n·pq/(pq+p+q) and must be integer ⇔ D=pq+p+q | n. For each N=M+c, allowed D must divide N: if 3|D ⇒ c≡0 (mod D); else c≡−1 (mod D). Choose distinct primes p,q maximizing 1/p+1/q (i.e. smallest p,q) subject to D|N. Compute r= pq/(pq+p+q); g(c)=⌊2025!·r⌋/2025!. Sum g’s → T/2025!; reduce to p/q; answer (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure D|N with the 3‑rule, use only prime p,q (not composites), and verify L integer (D|N). Use big integer 2025! for floor.

Insights: For N≥25, f(N) = min L≥⌈(N+3)/3⌉ with N−L = sum of two distinct proper divisors of L. Hence f(N)=N−s where s>0 but tiny (≤≈100). For huge M=3^{2025!}, any c≪M gives floor(2025!·f(M+c)/M)=2025!−1; for N=5M (c=4M) gives 5·2025!−1. Thus sum S=5(1−1/2025!)+(5−1/2025!)=10−6/2025! = (10·2025!−6)/2025!. Reduce by 6: p=(10·2025!−6)/6, q=2025!/6, coprime. Need (p+q) mod 99991 = ((11·2025!−6)/6) mod 99991. Compute 2025! mod (6·99991) then evaluate. Pitfall: ensure s>0 (f(N)<N) for all given N (true since N not multiple of 11). Use modular arithmetic with large factorial.

Insights: f(N)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=N. Minimal L/N ratio comes from triples (L, L/p, L/q) → ratio = pq/(pq+p+q). For each pair (p,q) compute D= (pq+p+q)/gcd(pq,pq+p+q); N must be multiple of D·(lcm(p,q)/(pq/gcd)). Smallest ratios in order: 6/11 (D=11), 4/7 (D=7), 10/17 (D=17), 3/5 (D=5), 2/3 (D=3). M=3^{2025!} ⇒ M≡1 (mod D) for D∤3, M≡0 (mod 3^k). Thus N=M+c ≡1+c (mod D) (D∤3), ≡c (mod 3). For given c’s: c=0 ⇒ only D=3 works → ratio 2/3. c=4M ⇒ N=5M ⇒ divisible by 5 only → ratio 3/5. Other c’s ≡4 (mod 5) and ≡0 (mod 3) but not ≡10 (mod 11),6 (mod 7),16 (mod 17) → best ratio 3/5. Hence g(0)=2/3, others=3/5. Sum=2/3+5·3/5=11/3 ⇒ p+q=14 ⇒ answer 14.

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. For M=3^K (K=2025!), the minimal LCM for n≈M is L₀=2/3 M (triple 3^{K‑2},2·3^{K‑2},L₀). Any n=M+c (c≪M) needs L₀+O(c); Δ≪M, so K·Δ/M<1 ⇒ floor unchanged. Thus g(c)=2/3 for all small c. For c=4M, n=5M, minimal LCM=10/3 M, giving g=10/3. Sum=2/3+10/3+4·2/3=20/3 ⇒ p+q=23 (mod 99991). Pitfall: ensure Δ never ≥M/K; for tiny c it isn’t.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n. For n=M+ c (M=3^N, N huge) optimal triple uses a common factor d=3^{v₃(c)} (or max ≤(M+c)/6). Then f(M+c)=d·f((M+c)/d). Since (M+c)/d≈3^{N‑v₃(c)} huge, its f≈(2/3)·(M+c)/d. Hence α_c=f(M+c)/M≈(2/3)(1+ c/M)/3^{v₃(c)}. Compute floor(2025!·α_c) for each c (0,4M,1848374,…). Use v₃(c) values (0,0,1,2,?); evaluate α_c exactly as fractions with denominator 3^{v₃(c)}. Sum floors → S. Reduce S/2025! → p/q. Finally compute (p+q) mod 99991. Pitfalls: ensure d respects distinctness (need (M+c)/d≥6); handle c=0 separately (use d=M/9). Use exact rational arithmetic; avoid assuming α=1 when c sum of two powers.

Insights: f(N)=min_{s|N} (L(s)/s) where L(s) is min LCM of three distinct numbers summing to s. Ratios R(s) are monotone by divisor: R(s)=min_{d|s}R(d). Small‑ratio “bases”: 11→6/11, 7→4/7, 17→10/17, 10→3/5, 23→15/23, 13→8/13, 25→16/25, primes≥31 give R(p)=L/p (e.g. 97→64/97, 103→68/103). For N=M+c (M=3^k), if s∤3 then s|N ⇔ s|(c+1); if 3|s then s|N ⇔ s|c. Thus g(c)=min R(s) over s dividing c+1 (coprime to 3) or c (multiple of 3). Compute for given c:  
c=0,4M → only 3‑powers → R=2/3.  
c=1848374,10162574 → c+1 divisible by 25 (best) → 16/25.  
c=265710644 → smallest coprime divisor≥6 is 97 → 64/97.  
c=44636594 → smallest coprime divisor≥6 is 103 → 68/103.  
Sum = 2/3+2/3+16/25+16/25+64/97+68/103 = 2947336/749325.  
(p+q) mod 99991 = 96985.  

Pitfalls: ignore s multiples of 3 (need c), ensure s≥6, use exact ratios (2025! cancels).

Insights: f(n)=min LCM(a,b,c) with a+b+c=n. For M=3^K (K=2025!), base L=2/3 M works (a=3^{K‑2},b=2·3^{K‑2},c=L). For any n=M+c, g(c)=⌊K!·f(M+c)/M⌋/K! = f(M+c)/M because f/M’s denominator is a power of 3 dividing K!. Thus g(c)=f(M+c)/M exactly. Known values: f(M)=2/3 M ⇒ g(0)=2/3. For n=5M (c=4M) f= (10/3)M ⇒ g(4M)=10/3. For all other given c (tiny vs M) f(M+c)=2/3 M (base works) ⇒ g=2/3. Sum = 2/3+10/3+4·2/3 = 20/3 ⇒ p+q=23. Pitfall: ensure f/M denominator divides K!; otherwise floor could truncate.

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{d|n, d≥6} (f(d)/d). For odd n, smallest odd divisor ≥7 decides ratio. f(p)=2⌊p/3⌋ for odd prime p (p≠3). Ratios: 11→6/11 (best), 7→4/7, then larger primes give larger ratios.  

M=3^{2025!}. For N=M (c=0) and N=5M (c=4M) smallest odd divisor≥6 is 9 ⇒ ratio = 2/3.  

For N=M+c with c≡2 (mod 3) (the other four c), M≡1 (mod p) for any p≤2025, p≠3, so N≡c+1 (mod p). Thus odd primes dividing N are exactly odd primes (≠3) dividing c+1.  

Factor c+1:  
1848375=3²·5³·31·53 → smallest odd divisor≥7 is 31 ⇒ ratio = 20/31.  
10162575=3²·5²·31²·47 → smallest ≥7 is 31 ⇒ ratio = 20/31.  
265710645=3³·5·97·103·197 → smallest ≥7 is 97 ⇒ ratio = 64/97.  
44636595=3·5·103·167·173 → smallest ≥7 is 103 ⇒ ratio = 68/103.  

Since K=2025! is divisible by each denominator (3,31,97,103), floor(K·p/q)=K·p/q.  

Sum g’s = 2·(2K/3)+2·(20K/31)+(64K/97)+(68K/103) = K·[4/3+40/31+64/97+68/103] = K·(3664288/929163).  

Thus p=3664288, q=929163 (coprime). Compute (p+q) mod 99991 = 93856.  

Pitfalls: ignore even divisors (N odd), exclude d=5 (sum<6), ensure K multiple of denominators.

Insights: f(N)=N·min_{s|N, s≥6}R(s) where R(s)=min_{a+b+c=s}lcm(a,b,c)/s. Smallest R(s): 6/11 (s multiple 11), 4/7 (s multiple 7), then 16/25 (s=25), 30/47, 64/97, 110/167.  

M=3^{2025!}≡1 (mod d) for any d coprime 3, so N=M+c is divisible by s⇔s|1+c.  

c=0 ⇒ N divisible only by 3‑powers → s=9, R=2/3 → g(0)=2/3.  
c=4M ⇒ N=5M, still divisible by 9 → R=2/3, f= (2/3)·5M → g=10/3.  

For c=1848374,10162574,265710644,44636594 compute 1+c factorisation (ignore 3‑factors). Smallest R(s) among its odd, non‑3 divisors:  

1848374: s=25 → R=16/25.  
10162574: s=47 → R=30/47.  
265710644: s=97 → R=64/97.  
44636594: s=167 → R=110/167.  

Thus sum S=2/3+10/3+16/25+30/47+64/97+110/167 = 125561848/19033825 (coprime).  

Answer: (p+q) mod 99991 = (125561848+19033825) mod 99991 = 8687.  

Pitfalls: ensure N not divisible by 2 or 3 (c even, M odd), use only s|1+c (coprime 3). Verify 2025! divisible by each s so g(c)=R(s).

Insights: f(N)=N·min_{d|N,d≥6}R(d) where R(d)=min LCM(a,b,c)/d. R(d) depends only on smallest “good” divisor of d: 11→6/11, 7→4/7, 17→10/17, 10→3/5, 23→22/23, 13→8/13, 25→16/25, … For M=3^{2025!}, M≡1 (mod p) for p≠3, so M+c divisible by p ⇔ p|c+1. c=0,4M give only 3‑powers ⇒ ratio 2/3. c+1 factors: 1848375=3²·5³·31·53 → min divisor≥6 not multiple of 3 is 25 ⇒ g=16/25. 10162575 same ⇒ g=16/25. 265710645=3³·5·97·103·197 → min divisor≥6 not multiple of 3 is 97 ⇒ g=64/97. 44636595=3·5·103·167·173 → min divisor≥6 not multiple of 3 is 103 ⇒ g=68/103. Sum =2/3+2/3+16/25+16/25+64/97+68/103=2947336/749325 (coprime). (p+q) mod 99991 = 96985.  

Pitfalls: ignore composite odd divisors (e.g., 25), ensure denominators ≤2025! so floor doesn’t truncate.

Insights: For N≥25 optimal triple includes its LCM L. So f(N)=min L≥⌈(N+3)/3⌉ with N−L = sum of two distinct proper divisors of L. For huge M=3^{2025!}, any N=M+c (c≪M) has f(N)=≈(6/11)N with error ≪ M/(2025!·6/11). Hence floor(2025!·f(N)/M)= (2025!·6/11)·⌊N/M⌋. Thus g(c)=6k/11 where k=⌊(M+c)/M⌋ (k=1 for five terms, k=5 for 4M). Sum =5·6/11+30/11=60/11 ⇒ p+q=71. Pitfall: assume f(N)≈6N/11 without proving error negligible; need bound that deviation≪M/(2025!·6/11).

Insights: f(n)=min lcm(a,b,c) for a+b+c=n ⇒ f(n)=n·min_{d|n, d≥6}(f(d)/d). For odd n, smallest odd divisor d≥6 gives the minimum; f(d)/d=2⌊d/3⌋/d. Thus ratio r(d) decreases with smaller d (except 5).  

Compute M=3^{2025!}.  

- M, 5M ⇒ smallest odd divisor 9 → r=2/3.  
- N=M+1848374, M+10162574: c+1 divisible by 5³,31,53 → N divisible by 25 (smallest ≥6) → r=16/25.  
- N=M+265710644: c+1 has 5·97·103 → smallest odd divisor 97 → r=64/97.  
- N=M+44636594: c+1 has 5·103 → smallest odd divisor 103 → r=68/103.  

Since 2025! is multiple of all denominators, g(c)=r exactly.  

Sum = 2·(2/3)+2·(16/25)+64/97+68/103 = 2947336/749325.  

p+q mod 99991 = 96985.   (Pitfall: ignore 5, use 25 when 5²|N.)
